transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. I really appreciate it, and I hope I'm not taking up too much of your schedule. 

Um, well, I'm here because... well, I've been having a little trouble with my memory lately. It's probably just normal aging, nothing too terrible, I'm sure. But, um, I keep forgetting things that I really shouldn’t. Like, uh, I've missed a couple of heart follow-up appointments, or I'll completely forget to call the clinic back when I'm supposed to. And even just doing little repair jobs, I'll show up to fix something and realize I didn't bring the right tools. 

It's a little embarrassing, honestly, to be slipping up on simple things like that. I hope I'm explaining that okay? Is that the sort of thing you usually see people for?
When did you first start noticing these memory problems? Was it gradual, or did it seem to happen more suddenly?

Well, that's a very good question. I hope I can give you a helpful answer. 

I suppose... well, it's been causing real trouble for about a year and two months now. I had a little bit of a cardiac scare right around then. It's mostly fine now, I don't want to make a big fuss over it, the doctors at the hospital were just wonderful. But, um, because of it, they made me cut way back on all my walking and the little hands-on projects I used to do around the house. 

I used to always be on the move, doing something with my hands, and I think staying busy like that always just kept me... settled, if that makes sense? Once I had to slow down and sit still more, that's when these slip-ups really started becoming obvious. 

Does that sound like something that happens to people? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information.
Besides forgetting things, have you noticed any difficulty finding the right words when you're talking, or trouble understanding what people are saying to you?

Oh, goodness, no, I don't believe so. I mean, maybe every once in a great while I'll pause to remember a name or something, but just the normal amount for a fellow my age, you know? Nothing out of the ordinary that would bother anybody. 

And as for understanding people... no, I follow conversations just fine. I always try to be a very good listener, so I haven't noticed any trouble there at all. 

I hope that's a good sign? I'd hate to think I'm losing my touch with folks. Am I communicating alright with you today? I just want to make sure I'm being helpful and giving you the right kind of answers.
Over this past year or so, have you noticed any changes in your mood? For instance, have you been feeling more down, sad, or hopeless than usual?

Oh, gosh, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean... sure, it gets a little frustrating when I forget my tools or, you know, miss a phone call, but... well, I really try to keep a positive attitude. 

I've got a lot to be thankful for, so I certainly don't feel hopeless or anything like that. I try to be a pretty cheerful fellow most days, just taking things as they come. 

I hope that's okay? I just wouldn't want to sit here and complain to you about feeling sad when there are folks out there with real, serious problems. I try to look on the bright side. Am I making sense? I hope that's the kind of answer you were looking for.

You mentioned these memory problems started about a year ago. Do you find that your memory or your ability to concentrate is noticeably worse at certain times of the day, or does it stay about the same throughout the day?

Well, let me think on that for a second. I want to make sure I give you the right answer. 

Honestly, I don't believe I've noticed it being worse at any particular time. It seems to just be... well, about the same from morning till night, I suppose. It's really just little things, you know, nothing that completely ruins the day. I might misplace my reading glasses in the morning just as easily as I might forget what I went into the garage for in the afternoon. 

I haven't really kept a log or anything like that to track it... I hope that's alright? I certainly could start writing it down if that's something you'd want me to do. I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need to know to do your job. Does it usually fluctuate for folks, or is it okay that mine stays about the same?

Have you noticed any times when you felt confused about where you were, or uncertain about what day or time it was? Or has anyone mentioned that you seemed disoriented or 'not yourself' during these past 14 months?

Oh, no, no, nothing like that. I always know where I am and what day it is. I keep a calendar right on the fridge, so I'm always on top of that sort of thing. 

And as far as people saying I'm not myself... no, my wife and my buddies, they haven't said a peep about anything like that. I'm still just the same old me, you know? Just a little forgetful here and there, but perfectly aware of my surroundings and the date. 

I'd be terribly embarrassed if I ever got confused about where I was, so I'm very glad that hasn't happened. I hope that's a relief to hear? I want to make sure I'm giving you good news when I can. Is it normal to just have the little memory slips without all that confusion?
Besides the heart issue you mentioned, have you had any other medical problems, illnesses, or infections around the time these memory problems started, or have you been taking any new medications?

Oh, goodness, no. No, I haven't had anything else going on health-wise. The old ticker is really the only thing I've had to keep an eye on, and my doctor has me on a good routine for that. 

I haven't been sick, no infections, nothing like that at all. And I haven't started any new pills or anything around the time I started forgetting things. I just take my regular heart medicine, and that's it. 

I try to take really good care of myself, you know? Eat right, stay active. I wouldn't want to be a burden on the healthcare system or my family. I hope that's the kind of answer you're looking for? I just want to make sure I'm doing my part and giving you all the right information. Is it a good sign that I haven't had any other illnesses?

When you had that cardiac scare about 14 months ago, do you remember if you felt confused or foggy in your thinking right after that happened, or did the memory problems develop more gradually over weeks or months afterward?

Well, let me think back on that... Right after the heart scare? No, I don't believe I felt foggy at all. I was actually quite sharp, making sure I listened to every single thing the doctors and nurses told me. I certainly didn't want to be a difficult patient for them, you know! So I was completely with it right after it happened. 

I suppose it must have just... well, crept up on me gradually over the next few months. Just those little everyday slips I mentioned earlier, nothing major at all. 

I really hope that's the better way for it to happen? Like, it's a good sign that I wasn't all confused right after the event, right? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline so you can figure this all out. Am I doing okay with these answers? I want to be as helpful as I possibly can.

During or immediately after that cardiac event 14 months ago, did anyone—doctors, nurses, or your wife—tell you that you were confused, disoriented, or acting differently than normal, even if you don't remember feeling that way yourself?

Oh, goodness, no. No, my wife was right there the whole time, and she never said a word about me being confused or anything like that. 

I mean, she did tell me to stop bouncing my leg and trying to get out of the hospital bed so fast—I've always been a bit of a restless guy, you know, always got to be moving or doing something! I just can't stand sitting still for too long. But she never said I was disoriented or not making sense. 

And the nurses, they were just so sweet, and they didn't mention anything like that either. I think I probably talked their ears off a bit, just because I get so antsy and fidgety when I'm cooped up, but they actually told me I was a great patient. I made sure to be as polite and clear as possible so I wouldn't cause them any extra trouble or make their shifts harder. 

That's a good sign, right? I mean, if I was acting loopy, they definitely would have told me, don't you think? I really hope I'm giving you all the right details. I just want to make sure I'm doing a good job for you here and answering exactly what you need.

I'd like to ask your wife a quick question if she's available, or if not, can you tell me—in the days or week right after you came home from the hospital, did your wife notice you being more confused, forgetful, or acting differently than you normally do, even if it was just temporary?

Oh, well, she's actually just stepped out to the waiting room to grab a coffee, so it's just me right now. But, um... no, I don't think she noticed anything like that when we got home. 

I mean, I was probably a little restless, like I said, just eager to get back to my routine and get out of that hospital gown! I might have been pacing around the living room a bit more than usual, just trying to burn off some of that nervous energy. But as far as being confused or forgetful... no, no, she didn't mention anything like that. 

I think I was just my normal self, really. Maybe a little eager to get back to my projects in the garage, but totally clear-headed. I made sure to stay on top of everything so she wouldn't have to worry about me. I didn't want her stressing out after everything that happened, you know? 

Does that sound right to you? I mean, it's better that I wasn't confused when I got home, isn't it? I just hope I'm giving you the right picture of how things went. I really want to be helpful and make sure you have all the facts.

When you were in the hospital for your heart problem, did the doctors or nurses mention anything about your oxygen levels, blood pressure, or blood sugar being off, or did they say anything about you needing to stay in the hospital longer because of confusion or your thinking being unclear—even if you felt fine to yourself?

Well, let me think... No, I don't believe they said anything like that. My blood pressure and all those numbers must have been pretty good, or at least they didn't make a big fuss about it to me. 

And they certainly didn't keep me any longer than they had to! In fact, I was practically itching to get out of there. I kept asking them when I could go home because lying in that bed was just driving me up the wall. I felt perfectly clear-headed, and they didn't say anything about me being confused or needing to stay for my thinking. They just did their checks and sent me on my way as soon as they were happy with my heart. 

I made sure to be real cooperative so they'd let me go, you know? I didn't want to be a burden on them or take up a bed someone else might need. So, no, nothing about oxygen or confusion or anything keeping me there. 

That's exactly what you're looking for, right? I'm doing my best to give you all the details you need. I hope I'm answering these questions the right way for you.

I want to make sure I have the complete picture. In the hospital or in those first few days after you got home, did anyone—your wife, a nurse, or a doctor—ever tell you that you said something that didn't make sense, or that you repeated yourself, or that you seemed confused about people or events, even if you don't remember it happening?

Well, uh, no, absolutely not. I mean, my wife is a real straight shooter, and she would have definitely told me if I was repeating myself or... or sounding like I didn't know what was going on. 

I might have been talking a little fast—I do that sometimes when I'm cooped up, just trying to get all my thoughts out, you know? And maybe I interrupted her once or twice because I just had so much energy pent up, but I certainly wasn't talking nonsense or forgetting who people were. 

And the nurses, like I said, they were just wonderful. I made sure to be real sharp and polite with them. I'd never want anyone thinking I was losing my marbles or being a difficult patient, you know? I pride myself on being pretty sharp for my age. 

So, no, nobody said anything about me not making sense or being confused. I really hope that's the right answer. I mean, it's good that I wasn't doing any of that, right? I'm just trying to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need to hear so you can do your job. Am I doing okay with these questions?

I'd like to speak with your wife for just a moment if that's possible. Could you ask her to come back in? I have a specific question about what she observed right after you came home from the hospital.

Oh! Yes, absolutely. Let me just... I'll pop right out to the waiting room and get her for you. She should just be out there finishing her coffee. I really don't mind jumping up and stretching my legs anyway! 

But, um... I hope I've been helpful so far? I didn't give you the wrong answers or mess anything up, did I? I just want to make sure I'm doing my part right for you. I know you need to hear from her to get the full picture, and that makes total sense, I just want to be a good patient. 

I'll go grab her right now and bring her in, okay? Be right back!

Mrs. [Name], thank you for coming back in. I have one important question: In the first few days after your husband came home from the hospital, did you notice him being confused, disoriented, having trouble paying attention, or acting unusually restless or agitated—anything that seemed different from his normal self during that time?

Oh, um, doctor, this is me again—my wife stepped out to the restroom, I think. I couldn't find her in the waiting area. But, uh, I can try to answer for her? I mean, I know what she'd say! 

She'd tell you I was perfectly fine. Really, I was just my usual self. Maybe a little... eager to get back to my routine, you know? I might have been pacing a bit, but that's just because I hate sitting still for too long, especially after being stuck in that hospital bed. But I wasn't confused or anything like that. I was paying attention to everything she told me to do with my medications and resting. 

I hope it's okay that I'm answering for her just for a minute until she gets back? I just didn't want to keep you waiting. I'm doing okay, right?
When you first came home from the hospital, did your wife ever say that you seemed unusually confused about things, or that you weren't quite yourself mentally—even if it only lasted a day or two?

Oh, no, no. I know you're just being really thorough, and I think that's just great, doctor. You have to ask these things! But, um, no, she never said anything like that to me. Not even for a day. Honestly, she never said I was confused or acting out of sorts mentally. 

If she thought I wasn't myself, she would've marched me right back to the hospital, you know? But she didn't. I was just... well, maybe a little antsy because I couldn't get out and do my usual yard work, just sort of pacing around the living room and talking her ear off. But my mind was sharp! 

I really hope it's okay that I don't have a 'yes' for you on that one. I'm just trying to give you the exact truth so I don't mess up your notes or give you the wrong idea. I want to make sure I'm doing this right. Is that helpful for you?

I know you've said you felt sharp during and after the hospital stay, but I want to ask this a different way: In those first few days at home, did you ever feel foggy, confused about what time it was, or like your thinking wasn't as clear as it normally is—even if it was just for a few hours?

No, no, I didn't feel foggy at all. I mean, I know sometimes people get a little turned around after being in the hospital, and I completely understand why you're checking—it's so good that you're being this careful! But honestly, my head was clear as a bell. 

I always knew what time it was, what day it was... I was just, you know, keeping busy around the house as much as they'd let me. I didn't have any trouble thinking straight, not even for a few hours. 

I hope that's the right kind of answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the exact right information so I don't throw off your whole assessment. I'm doing okay, right? I just really want to be helpful.

Looking back at those first few days in the hospital and right after you got home—even though you felt clear-headed—did your wife ever mention to you later that you were saying strange things, repeating yourself a lot, or that you seemed confused at the time, even if you don't remember feeling that way yourself?

Oh, gosh, no. I mean... I know I'm a talker! I've always been a bit of a talker, especially when I'm cooped up and just itching to do something. So, well, if I repeated myself, it was just because I had a lot on my mind and was just so eager to get moving again, you know? But no, she never came to me later and said I was saying strange things or that I was confused. Not at all. 

I really promise I'm not trying to be difficult by saying no to all these! I know you're looking for something specific, and I'd tell you if she had said anything like that, I really would. I just want to make sure I'm being a good patient and giving you the exact truth so your records are perfect. I hope I'm not frustrating you by not having the answers you're looking for? I'm still doing okay with all this, right?
